Abbot of the Chan Temple of the World’s Virtue (Shan-shi Ch’an-ssu) in the Great Ming Heavenly Realm,
and the Subject Monk Ruxi, Abbot of the Yanfu Lecture Temple (Yan-fu Jiang-ssu).
"Furthermore, Mahāmati, it is not that there is no resemblance to illusion; rather, one perceives all phenomena as being like an illusion.
Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is it because of attachment to various illusory appearances that you say all dharmas are like illusions?
Or is it because of attachment to distinct characteristics?”
If one clings to various illusory appearances and asserts that all natures are like illusions, World-Honored One,
there would be natures that are not like illusions. Why is this so?
That is to say, Blessed One, the various characteristics of form are not caused;
there is no cause for the various characteristics of form to appear as they do, like a magical illusion.
“World-Honored One!
For this reason, there is no attachment to various illusory appearances as being similar to illusion.

Previously it was said that all dharmas are like illusions; the Buddha, fearing that Mahāmati might doubt why illusion alone is used as a metaphor, further declared: “It is not merely by means of the metaphor of illusion that all dharmas are [described]; rather, because there is nothing else with which they can be compared, it is said that all dharmas are like illusions.”

In this third question, the intention is as follows: when the Buddha says that all phenomena are like illusions, does he mean they are "like illusions" because one clings to various illusory appearances, or does he mean they are "like illusions" because one does not cling to any appearances?

If one clings to illusory appearances and claims that all phenomena are like illusions, it does not necessarily follow that all phenomena are indeed like illusions; therefore, it is said that "there are natures that are not like illusions," where "nature" refers to the phenomena themselves.
Furthermore, the intention of the challenger’s objection is as follows:

if one speaks in general terms, all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) should have no distinct causes; yet, in the world, there has never been a single caused phenomenon that is entirely like an illusion.
After the World-Honored One had descended, the objections were formulated as in the text.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"It is not that all phenomena, which resemble various illusory appearances due to clinging to them, are like illusions."
Mahāmati!
However, all unreal dharmas perish as swiftly as lightning; thus, they are like illusions. Mahāmati!

For example, like a flash of lightning that appears for a mere moment and vanishes as soon as it has appeared—yet this is not perceived by the foolish—in the same way, all natures are merely the self-imaginations of one's own mind regarding their specific and general characteristics.
Upon investigation, they are found to lack intrinsic nature; they are not the manifestation of objective forms to which one becomes attached.

In the response, the statement that "all phenomena are like illusions" does not mean one is actually attached to the characteristics of illusion; rather, it is simply because all phenomena are unreal and perish as swiftly as lightning that they are said to be like illusions.

Furthermore, a simile is used to illustrate the speed with which a flash of lightning arises and ceases in a single moment; this is known only by noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), and is not a manifest phenomenon perceived by the ignorant.
As stated below in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*:

"All phenomena appear based on one's own discrimination as individual and common characteristics, and it is likewise thus. Because they are unable to contemplate their non-existence, they falsely conceptualize and cling to various forms and appearances."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"There is no analogy for that which is not illusion; The nature of dharmas is said to be like an illusion, Unreal and as swift as lightning; Therefore, they are said to be like illusions."
The first two lines answer that there is nothing non-illusory with which to metaphorize all phenomena; the latter two lines answer that the characteristics of illusion are like lightning.
Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As the World-Honored One has taught that all natures are unarisen and like illusions, will there not be a contradiction between what the World-Honored One has previously and subsequently stated?"
"Why do you say that the nature of non-arising is like an illusion?

This fourth question means: since the Buddha has stated that all phenomena are non-existent because they are unarisen, yet also said they are existent because they are like illusions, is this not a contradiction between existence and non-existence?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"It is not my teaching that the nature of non-arising is like an illusion that incurs the fault of contradiction between earlier and later statements. Why is this so?
That is to say, regarding birth as non-birth, one awakens to the fact that it is merely the manifestation of one's own mind;
that existence and non-existence, external nature and the absence of nature, are non-arising manifestations.
Mahāmati!

It is not that my previous and subsequent statements are contradictory; rather, it is because I wish to destroy the externalists' view of arising from causes that I teach that all natures are unarisen. Mahāmati!
The deluded masses of externalists desire for existence and non-existence to arise, yet this is not due to the conditions of their own various conceptual attachments and false imaginings.
"Mahāmati!
I do not arise from existence or non-existence; therefore, I speak by means of the teaching of non-arising.
This is the response to the Buddha’s refutation of the contradiction in my [previous] statement, providing both an inquiry and an explanation.
"Birth is non-birth" means that I have realized birth itself is non-birth, because it is merely what is manifested by one's own mind.
Whether existent or non-existent, all external phenomena are fundamentally without the nature of arising; therefore, I speak of non-birth.
This is the general answer.
Within the specific answer, there are two parts:

first, to destroy the arising from causes as conceived by non-Buddhists—for instance, because they reckon that various distinct causes give rise to existence—it is taught that all natures are unarisen; [second, to demonstrate the nature of reality].
Second, it is to refute the heterodox views that posit the existence or non-existence of birth, rather than being based on one's own attachment to deluded conceptualization as a causal condition.

Furthermore, when [the Buddha] told Mahāmati, "I am neither existent nor non-existent," it means that because he is free from the views of existence and non-existence, he teaches non-arising by means of the doctrine of non-arising.

“Mahāmati! As for the teaching on ‘nature’ (svabhāva), it is for the purpose of encompassing birth and death; for the purpose of destroying the view of non-existence and the view of annihilationism; and for the purpose of causing my disciples to encompass various karmas and places of rebirth. Thus, by means of the term ‘nature,’ I teach the encompassing of birth and death.”
Regarding the explanation of nature (*dhātu*), the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states:

"The teaching of all phenomena is intended to cause disciples to understand that they undergo birth and death through the grasping of various karmas, and to prevent them from falling into the views of existence, non-existence, annihilation, or nihilism."
The phrase "for my disciples" is used below to inform the disciples that they receive birth according to their karma.

Regarding the term "nature-sound" (*xing-sheng*): "nature" (*xing*) refers to the Dharma, and "sound" (*sheng*) refers to its exposition; it means that by expounding the Dharma, one explains the encompassing of birth and death.
“Mahāmati, I speak of the characteristics of the self-nature of illusion in order to lead one away from attachment to the characteristics of self-nature.

Fools fall into the characteristics of evil views and longings; they do not understand that things are merely manifestations of their own minds, and they are attached to the characteristics of self-nature produced by causes and conditions. They destroy [the truth] by clinging to the notion that things arise through causal agency.”

I teach that all phenomena have the nature and characteristics of illusions and dreams, so as not to allow foolish people with evil views and expectations to become attached to themselves and all other phenomena, and thus produce incorrect doctrines by failing to see things as they truly are.
"Mahāmati!
To see all dharmas as they truly are means to transcend the manifestation of one's own mind.
The passage beginning with "explaining the nature of illusion" below explains the meaning of the term "illusion."
Because the nature of all things is detached, one knows that the nature of illusion is itself detachment from self-nature.
This is what the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra* means when it says, "Knowing illusion is itself detachment."
The second is for the purpose of destroying the grasping at signs by foolish people; this further consists of three aspects:

first, not knowing that [all things] are merely the manifestations of one's own mind; second, subverting the phenomena produced from correct causes and conditions; and third, clinging to the signs of self-nature as being substantially real. Therefore, it is taught that all dharmas have the characteristics of being like illusions and dreams in order to destroy these [graspings].

It does not allow the foolish to descend [into error]; rather, it attributes faults [to others] while manifesting its own virtues. To engage in incorrect discourse regarding the state of reality as it truly is constitutes the attribution of fault.
This incorrect discourse consists of the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) that clings to the intrinsic nature of self and other.
Furthermore, "abiding in reality as it is" (yathābhūta-sthāna) reveals its excellence.
The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states:
"One who sees all phenomena as they truly abide is one who has realized that [all things] are manifestations of mind-only."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“The unarisen is the non-existence of being; existence encompasses birth and death.
Observing them as like illusions and the like, one does not form false imaginings regarding their marks.”
Regarding "non-arising constitutes the absence of nature," the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"Because there is no activity, there is no arising.
This means that the nature of all phenomena is fundamentally without arising; therefore, it is called "non-arising."
"Existence encompasses birth and death"—this verse refers to birth and death as being based on karma.
To view them through the contemplation of their being like an illusion is to be free from deluded conceptualization and discrimination.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!"
I shall now explain the characteristics of the groups of names (*nāmakāya*), phrases (*padakāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*).

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who skillfully contemplate the groups of names, phrases, and phonemes will accordingly enter into the meanings, phrases, and phonemes, and swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Having awakened in this way, one awakens all sentient beings.
Mahāmati! As for "name-body" (nāmakāya), it refers to the establishment of names based upon things; this is called the name-body.
Regarding the "body of phrases" (*padakāya*): it refers to a phrase that possesses a body of meaning, wherein its intrinsic nature is determined and finalized;
this is called the body of phrases. Regarding the "body of phonemes" (*vyañjanakāya*): it refers to that which manifests names and phrases; this is called the body of phonemes.
Furthermore, the "body of form" (*rūpakāya*) refers to length, shortness, height, and depth.
Furthermore, the "body of phrases" (*padakāya*) refers to tracks; for example, the tracks left by elephants, horses, humans, beasts, and so forth receive the name "body of phrases."

Mahāmati! As for "name" (nāman) and "form" (rūpa): it is called "name" because one speaks of the four formless aggregates by means of names; it is called "form" because their own-characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) appear. These are termed the body of names, phrases, and forms (nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya).
"One should study the definitions and boundaries of the bodies of names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*).
Regarding these "bodies of names, phrases, and phonemes," the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states:
"Names signify intrinsic nature; phrases signify distinctions."
The *vyañjana* (phoneme) is the syllable (*akṣara*), which serves as the basis for the two [the word and the sentence].
The *ākṛti* (form) is the *vyañjana*.
The term "body" (*kāya*) has the meaning of a collection (*saṃghāta*).
Regarding "names (nāman) express intrinsic nature": for example, when speaking of the six sense faculties, one merely uses the names eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Regarding "phrases (pada) express distinctions": for example, saying that the eye is the Buddha-eye, the Dharma-eye, the wisdom-eye, and so forth, according to their various distinctions.
However, these three—name, phrase, and phoneme—are termed the "three provisional bodies.
Provisionality is spoken of in contrast to reality; thus, sound is the reality. This one reality and three provisionalities constitute the essence of the teaching as that which expresses.

Now, although it is simply stated that one "should explain the bodies of names, phrases, and phonemes," and not explicitly mentioned as "the single reality," this is because the sound of the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma is itself the single reality.

"One who observes well" means that by skillfully observing the teachings that express—namely, the bodies of names, phrases, and phonemes—one attains mastery of the meanings they express, swiftly accomplishing Bodhi; thus, one not only awakens oneself but is also able to awaken others.
The above constitutes the general explanation.
From "Great Wisdom" (*Mahāmati*) onwards, there follows the specific explanation.
That which is established as a name based on a thing refers to the fact that a name expresses its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Regarding "the phrase possesses the body of meaning," this refers to the phrase's function of expressing specific distinctions.

Generally, the nature of a phrase consists in expressing the distinctions among meanings; thus, it is definitive and ultimate, without confusion or overlap—this is the efficacy of the "body" (kāya) of the phrase.

Regarding the statement that "the formal body refers to the manifestation of names and phrases": this means that names and phrases are manifested by means of syllables, and conversely, names and phrases constitute the syllables; therefore, it is said that the syllable (*vyañjana*) is identical to the letter (*akṣara*), serving as the basis for both.
Furthermore, "form" (*rūpa*) is a metaphor; it is like the forms of people, which may be long or short, tall or low, and the length of a literary passage is likewise so.

As for the term "phrase-body" (*padakāya*), it refers to a "track" or "footprint": just as one first knows that elephants, horses, or other animals have passed by because of their tracks, so too does one find the meaning by following the phrases.
The Master then spoke in terms of forms and phrases.

If names are spoken in relation to forms, it is like the five aggregates—feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—where four aggregates are formless yet possess names, while the aggregate of form is said to have form because its own characteristics manifest; this is also like how written characters become manifest through their meanings.

The Buddha’s exposition of these bodies of names, phrases, and syllables is a gateway shown to learners for entering into the principle; since the principle is manifested through practice, it is said that "one should cultivate and study them."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“Regarding the distinctions between the body of names, the body of phrases, and the body of phonemes,
the foolish and ignorant cling to them, like an elephant sinking into deep mud.”
"The nature of words is detached from [inherent existence], which is itself liberation.
If one gives rise to views based on the words, the fault is the same as that of heterodox outsiders.
It is like an elephant sinking into deep mud; can one not be cautious?"
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
In a future age, those who possess wisdom will, having abandoned the views of identity, difference, both, or neither, question those lacking wisdom regarding the meaning of my established doctrine."
He replied: "This is not a correct question.

That is to say, regarding whether form (*rūpa*) and so forth are permanent or impermanent, and whether they are different or not different; likewise, regarding *nirvāṇa* and conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and the characterized (*lakṣya*), quality (*guṇa*) and the possessor of quality (*guṇin*), the primary element (*bhūta*) and the derivative (*bhautika*), the seer (*draṣṭṛ*) and the seen (*dṛśya*), gross objects (*sthūla*) and atoms (*paramāṇu*), as well as cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and the cultivator (*bhāvaka*)—such reciprocal relations as these.

Regarding such questions, it is said that the Buddha declared them "undetermined" (*avyākṛta*) and ceased the discussion, because they are not within the capacity of those foolish people to understand—namely, because they lack the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).

Because the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha wishes to cause them to depart from phrases that provoke fear, he declares these matters to be indeterminate (avyākṛta) and does not provide an explanation.
Furthermore, because it would serve to reinforce the speculative views of the non-Buddhists, he does not speak of them.
The Buddha taught that departing from the four propositions is fundamentally intended to lead one back to the correct path; therefore, he said to Mahāmati:

"In future ages, Bodhisattvas should question those people of the world by means of departing from the characteristics of the four propositions, intending thereby to demonstrate the gateway for entering the Way."
Those ignorant people, failing to comprehend this meaning, reply that this is not a correct treatise.

As for the statement "regarding form and so forth," it means that within the various dharmas such as the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), one distinguishes the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) of permanence and impermanence, difference and non-difference, and so on.

In this way, for those who practice toward nirvāṇa, their practice is itself able to manifest the practice of nirvāṇa—namely, the grasper and the grasped, the substratum and that which is supported, the creator and the created, and the seer and the seen.
"Dust and subtle dust" refers to the subtle dust of a lump of clay.
"Cultivation and the cultivator" refer to person and dharma.
"Thus, by way of such successive characteristics" refers to the two dharmas mentioned above in relation to one another.
Regarding these and other such matters, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:

"When questions are posed in this manner concerning things that are not to be declared, the World-Honored One declares that they should be answered with a suspension of the response; for such matters are beyond the capacity of the ignorant to understand."
The Buddha did not provide a definitive explanation because he wished to keep them from a state of fear and alarm. "Mahāmati!
The non-Buddhists speak thus, asserting that the life-principle is identical to the body; such are their indeterminate (avyākṛta) doctrines."
"Mahāmati!
Those various non-Buddhists, being deluded regarding causes, propound the doctrine of the indeterminate; this is not what I teach, Mahāmati."
That which I teach is free from the grasped and the grasper, wherein false conceptualization does not arise.
How, Mahāmati, is that [conceptualization] brought to rest? Mahāmati!
Those who are attached to the grasped and the grasper do so because they do not understand that all is a manifestation of one's own mind; therefore, they are brought to cessation.
Mahāmati, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas teach the Dharma to sentient beings by means of the four kinds of categorical discourse.
“Mahāmati!
As for the ‘discourse of setting aside’ (*sthāpanīya-praśna*), I have taught it from time to time for those whose faculties are not yet mature, but not for those who are mature.

As for the ‘discourse of refuting the views of non-Buddhists,’ because people generate interpretations based on mere words and cling to them as established views, I set these aside and do not speak of them, so that they may contemplate them and realize them for themselves.”

Regarding the claim that "life is identical to the body," because non-Buddhists calculate that the self is either identical to the aggregates (*skandha*) or distinct from the aggregates, they speak of the body and life as being one or different; such statements are called the "indeterminate theories" (*avyākṛta-vāda*).
Regarding those who formulate indeterminate theories concerning causes, they maintain that things arise without a cause; this is what is termed "indeterminate.
However, that which the Buddha has taught is free from the grasped and the grasper, and does not give rise to false conceptualization.
Regarding "how he stops them": why does he not simply speak directly in this manner to enlighten and stop them?
It is because they are merely attached to the grasper and the grasped, and do not know that these are manifestations of mind-only; therefore, he stops them.
The four types of discourse are as described in the subsequent text, and the discourse on cessation (*śamatha*) is one of them.
It is not only for the sake of refuting those non-Buddhists, but is also taught at times for those whose faculties are not yet mature.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
All dharmas are free from being produced by causes and conditions; they do not arise, for there is no agent. Therefore, Mahāmati, all dharmas are unarisen."
For what reason are all natures devoid of intrinsic nature?
Because when one examines them through self-awakened insight, neither individual nor common characteristics can be apprehended; therefore, it is said that all phenomena are unarisen.
Why are all phenomena (dharmas) neither to be brought nor to be taken away?

Because when one attempts to bring their specific or general characteristics (svalakṣaṇa/sāmānyalakṣaṇa), there is nowhere from which they come; and when one attempts to take them away, there is nowhere to which they go. Therefore, all phenomena are free from bringing and taking away.
Mahāmati! Why are all dharmas not extinguished?
It is because the characteristics of the self-nature of things do not exist; since all dharmas are unattainable, all dharmas are not extinguished.
Mahāmati! For what reason are all dharmas impermanent?
It is because their characteristics arise with the nature of impermanence; therefore, it is said that all dharmas are impermanent.
Mahāmati! For what reason are all dharmas eternal?
It is because their nature is the non-arising of characteristics; since the non-eternal is itself eternal, all dharmas are said to be eternal.
Below "all dharmas," the phrase "non-arising" is clarified with one primary meaning:
first, they do not arise because they are free from causes and conditions of action;
second, they do not arise because they are free from the characteristics of individual and common natures.

It cannot be brought down; for while, in terms of phenomena, there is no absence of coming and going, because one cannot find self- or common-characteristics when seeking them through the four propositions, no traces of coming or going are perceived.
The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states:
"Those who come have nowhere from which they come; those who go likewise have nowhere to which they go.
This is spoken in terms of principle (*li*).
That all phenomena are non-extinguished means that all dharmas are fundamentally devoid of intrinsic nature and characteristics; how could there be extinction?

The phrases "permanent" and "impermanent" are spoken in terms of both principle and emotion. If one speaks from the perspective of emotional perception, where characteristics and appearances undergo flux, it is said that the arising of characteristics is impermanent.
If one speaks from the perspective of principle, wherein every dharma is identical to its nature, it is said that the arising of characteristics is non-arising; this very impermanence is permanence.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"There are four kinds of formal discourse:
the categorical, the interrogative, the analytical, and the refutative; these are employed to subdue all non-Buddhists."
The Sāṃkhya and Vaiśeṣika teachers assert that existence and non-existence arise;
they demonstrate all things as being indeterminate.
Yet, that which is discerned by the Perfectly Awakened One has no inherent nature (svabhāva) that can be apprehended.
"Because it is free from verbal expression, it is said to be devoid of intrinsic nature.
Regarding these four types of discourse: that which is spoken with directness is called a "straightforward answer," meaning one answers in accordance with the question;
that which involves a counter-interrogation is also called "counter-objection," meaning one returns the question to the interlocutor.
"Analysis" (vibhajya-vyākaraṇa) refers to answering by means of detailed discernment;

"refusal to debate" (sthāpanīya-vyākaraṇa) refers to setting aside the question without answering. The various non-Buddhists (tīrthika) frequently employ the method of refusal to debate. Regarding "existence," "non-existence," and "arising":

the Sāṃkhya school calculates existence, while the Vaiśeṣika school calculates non-existence. "Sāṃkhya" refers to the School of Enumeration, and "Vaiśeṣika" refers to the School of Distinction. Such doctrines as these are all subsumed under the category of indeterminate discourse (avyākṛta-vyākaraṇa).
Those non-Buddhists reckon that there is neither arising nor non-arising; thus it is said, "they manifest in such a manner.
When observed with correct wisdom, their essential nature and characteristics cannot be found, let alone their verbal expressions.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I pray that you will explain for us the specific characteristics and the general characteristics of the various distinctions among the *srotāpannas* and their paths.”

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva skillfully understands the specific characteristics and general marks of the various paths of the *srotāpanna*, as well as the skillful means and characteristics of the *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, and *arhat*, and having distinguished and known them, preaches the Dharma for sentient beings in such and such ways—namely, the two marks of selflessness and the purification of the two obstacles—and attains the ultimate penetration of the characteristics of the various stages, reaching the inconceivable, ultimate realm of all Tathāgatas.

"Just as a mani jewel of manifold colors is well able to benefit all sentient beings, so too [the Buddha] sustains and nourishes all through the inexhaustible body and wealth of the objective realm of all dharmas.
Mahāmati is a follower of the Mahāyāna; why, then, does he request an explanation of the Hīnayāna?

In brief, there is a distinction between the Bodhisattva’s own practice and his transformation of others: while his own practice leads solely toward the ultimate fruit, the Dharma for transforming others must reach everywhere; therefore, at the request of the assembly, he expounded the Dharma of the four fruits.
*Srotāpanna* (須陀洹) is translated here as "Stream-enterer" (*yùliú*); it is the first fruit (*phala*).
Furthermore, regarding the term *srotāpanna-pratipannaka* (須陀洹趣), *pratipannaka* means "approaching" or "tending toward," referring to one who is heading toward the first fruit.

Regarding the "differentiated common characteristics" (*viśeṣa-sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), "common" (*sāmānya*) means identical; that is, one should thoroughly understand and discern both the common characteristics and the differentiated characteristics.

Furthermore, having attained a skillful understanding and discernment of the characteristics of the second, third, and fourth fruits, as well as the characteristics of the expedient means of cultivation.
"Thus it is, thus it is" means that one discriminates in this way and knows in this way.

For the sake of all sentient beings, one teaches these four dharmas so that they may realize the two characteristics of selflessness, purify the two obstacles of afflictions and knowledge, gradually penetrate the characteristics of the various stages (*bhūmi*), and attain the realm of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
The Dharma-body and the wealth of the Dharma benefit sentient beings inexhaustibly, just as a mani jewel provides for people with its treasures without depletion.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Listen attentively!"
"Listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well; I shall now speak for you.
Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent, World-Honored One!
We shall indeed listen and receive [your teaching].
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“There are three types of distinctions regarding the srotāpanna and the fruit of stream-entry.
What are the three?
They are the inferior, the middling, and the superior.”
The inferior [practitioner] will undergo at most seven more births;
the middling one will attain parinirvāṇa after three or five births;
the superior one will attain parinirvāṇa in that very life.

Regarding the answer that within the first fruit (*srotāpatti-phala*) there are three distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior: this refers merely to the differences in the sharpness or dullness of one's faculties (*indriya*).

As for "at most seven more births," this refers to those of the extremely dull, lowest faculty who, having severed the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-heya-kleśa*) and realized the first fruit, subsequently proceed to sever the delusions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*). Within the desire realm, they undergo seven cycles of birth and death while severing the nine grades of these delusions of cultivation, only then severing them to realize the third fruit (*anāgāmi-phala*).
Regarding "seven times": this refers to seven births among humans, seven births among devas, and fourteen births in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), totaling twenty-eight births.
The present mention of "seven times" is an abbreviation.

"Those with three or five births" refers to individuals of medium capacity who, after realizing the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), exhaust these afflictions through three or five births and thereby attain the realization of the third fruit (*anāgāmin*).

Regarding those who attain parinirvāṇa in that very life: this refers to individuals of superior faculties who, having attained the first fruit, transcend directly to the fourth fruit within that same lifetime and enter the nirvāṇa of true emptiness.
"These three types have three grades of fetters: inferior, middling, and superior.
What are the three fetters?

They are the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Through these distinctions among the three fetters, one progresses through the higher and higher stages to attain arhatship."

The three fetters (saṃyojana) are precisely those abandoned upon entering the first fruit; they are identical to the delusions of view (dṛṣṭi-kleśa) and the eighty-eight proclivities (anuśaya), differing only in their degree of elaboration or brevity.

As for the statement that they are also categorized as inferior, middling, and superior, this is because the fetters and delusions are divided into these three grades according to the faculties and dispositions of individuals.

Regarding "successively ascending" (*shàngshàng shèngjìn*) and so forth: within this process of abandoning afflictions and realizing the fruits, there are three types of abandonment and four types of leaping-over (*chāo*).
The term "successively ascending" is spoken in reference to the great leaping-over of those with superior faculties (*mūla-śakti*).

“Mahāmati, there are two kinds of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (the view of a self-existing body): namely, that which is innate (*sahaja*) and that which is conceptual (*parikalpita*), just as there are the conceptualization of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and the conceptualization of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

For example, based upon the intrinsic nature of dependent origination, various attachments to the intrinsic nature of conceptualization arise. Because they are neither existent nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, and because they lack the characteristics of real conceptualization, fools conceptually construct and become attached to the characteristics of various conceptualized intrinsic natures, like a deer perceiving water in a mirage at the time of summer heat.”

This is the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*). His false discrimination regarding the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is eliminated through the realization of the non-existence [of a person] by means of the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), thereby severing his long-standing ignorance and attachment.
As for the "view of a self," it is the perception of a sovereign master within the body of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
This is divided into two types:

the innate (*sahaja*) refers to that which arises simultaneously with the view and the body, such as the aforementioned view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*); furthermore, false conceptualization (*parikalpita*) arises based on this view, such as the aforementioned extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). Therefore, it is said to be "like dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*), meaning that the nature of false conceptualization (*parikalpitasvabhāva*) arises in dependence upon dependent origination.

The passage beginning with "Because those do not exist" correctly explains the aforementioned body-view of false imagination; since there are four views where originally there were none, they are thus the unreal marks of false imagination.

Just as in that dependent origination, because of their deluded imaginings, fools give rise to various attachments to the imagined nature; thus, it is likened to a mirage at the time of heat, where what is not water is called water—this is its characteristic mark.

Regarding those who grasp at the absence of intrinsic nature through the selflessness of persons: it is because those on the path toward the first fruit, by means of the contemplation of the selflessness of persons, realize that [phenomena] are fundamentally without intrinsic nature that their afflictions are severed.
When it is said "ignorance," it refers to defiled ignorance.

"Mahāmati, that which is innate [ignorance]—namely, the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) of a stream-enterer—is abandoned because the four aggregates of self and others lack the characteristic of form; because form arises from the primary elements and their derivatives; because they are mutually dependent causes and conditions; and because the primary elements and form do not aggregate. When the stream-enterer contemplates the categories of existence and non-existence, these do not appear, and thus the view of a self-body is severed."
"In this way, when the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is severed, craving does not arise; this is called the characteristic of the view of a self-body.

Regarding the innate view of a self-body: it is because a person who has attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) observes that the four aggregates (*skandha*) of their own and others' bodies—feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—are devoid of the characteristic of form.
Form arises from the four great elements; "the primary and the derived" refers to the producers and the produced, meaning that the aggregate of form is produced by the four great elements.
"Mutually dependent" means that the four great elements serve as causes for one another.
As for "non-accumulation," it means that the great elements and the nature of form do not coalesce.
Observing in this way, neither the existence nor the non-existence of the five aggregates can be apprehended; how, then, could there be the view of a self?
Therefore it is said: "The categories of existence and non-existence do not appear.
Once the view of a self-identity is severed, craving no longer arises.
"Mahāmati!..."

Regarding the characteristic of doubt: because one has attained the excellent vision of the characteristics of the Dharma, and because the two previous types of false imaginings regarding the view of a self-body have been severed, doubt regarding the Dharma does not arise; one no longer gives rise to the view of another as a Great Teacher for the sake of purification or impurity. This is called the characteristic of doubt severed by the Srotāpanna.

Regarding these characteristics of doubt: it is said that one who has attained the first fruit (srotāpanna) has clearly realized the Four Noble Truths without delusion, which constitutes the characteristic of "seeing well. Furthermore, because the two aforementioned types of self-view (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) have been abandoned through discernment, they no longer give rise to doubt regarding any phenomena. They naturally distinguish between the false and the correct, and no longer conceive of other non-Buddhist teachers as being Great Masters.
Regarding "purity and impurity," one does not harbor doubt concerning what is wholesome or unwholesome regarding the Buddha; this is the non-arising of the characteristic of doubt.
"Mahāmati! As for the clinging to precepts, why does a srotāpanna not cling to precepts?"
This means that because they clearly perceive the characteristics of suffering in the place of rebirth, they do not grasp at it. Mahāmati!
"Grasping" refers to the fool’s resolute undertaking of ascetic practices for the sake of the pleasure of various requisites, seeking rebirth thereby.

He does not grasp at them, except for the dedication toward the excellence of self-awakening; he practices the branches of the precepts through skillful means that are free from false conceptualization and characterized by the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) nature of phenomena. This is called the Stream-enterer’s severance of grasping at the marks of the precepts.
"Adherence to precepts" refers to regarding what is not a true precept as a precept.
It is the perverse habit of non-Buddhists who misidentify what is not a cause as a cause, such as observing the precepts of the chicken or the dog.

Those who have attained the first fruit do not adopt those precepts; that is to say, they clearly perceive the characteristics of suffering inherent in receiving retribution for such practices, and thus see them as merely a wearying exertion of asceticism, and so do not adopt them.
As for the foolish who do adopt them, they regard the various requisites of the five desires as pleasure, and therefore seek rebirth.
However, this is not the bliss of samādhi; though one may seek the fruit of bliss, what substance actually exists therein?

Those who have attained the first fruit do not take this [bliss] as their precept, yet it is not that they lack the precepts they themselves uphold. Therefore, it is said that by "excluding dedication toward self-awakening and the superior," one means that the preceptual practices cultivated by those individuals dedicate the cause toward the fruit.
Regarding the "limbs of morality" (*śīlāṅga*), "limb" refers to a constituent part, as in the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) or the five-limbed morality (*pañcāṅga-śīla*).
Although one does not adopt those [other categories] but adopts these, they are not the non-appropriating morality of the Mahāyāna; nevertheless, they are still forms of appropriation.
“The Srotāpanna has severed the three fetters, and craving and delusion do not arise.
If the Srotāpanna were to think,
‘I am not possessed of these fetters,’ there would be two faults:”
"They fall into the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and do not sever the various fetters (saṃyojana).
Mahāmati said to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One!"
The World-Honored One has spoken of many forms of craving; which among them is the craving that must be severed?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:

“It is the attachment and clinging to women, through various skillful means involving the evil karma of body and speech, whereby one experiences pleasure in the present while sowing the seeds of suffering for the future.”
That [craving] does not arise. Why is this?
Because one has attained the bliss of the correct reception of samādhi; therefore, that craving is severed, yet it is not the severance of the craving for nirvāṇa.
The "three fetters" mentioned refer to the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).
By severing these views, one becomes free from greed, hatred, and delusion.
These three [afflictions] are precisely the afflictions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) within the category of the delusions of view.

Regarding the mention of "two faults," the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the root, while the various fetters (*saṃyojana*) are the branches. Since the root is not eliminated, by what means could the branches be extinguished?

Greed has many varieties; specifically, the attachment to women is mentioned because it is the most prominent, cited here as the gravest instance. One who has attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) can sever such desire through the superior bliss of meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Although one is detached from existence, one still clings to emptiness; therefore, it is said that this is not the attainment of Nirvana through the severance of craving.
"Mahāmati, what are the characteristics of a Sakṛdāgāmin?"

This means that by suddenly illuminating the false imaginings of the marks of form, the arising-mark and the seeing-mark do not arise; because one skillfully perceives the characteristics of the progression toward dhyāna, one comes suddenly to this world and attains nirvana at the exhaustion of the limits of suffering; for this reason, one is called a sakṛdāgāmin.
This clarifies the characteristics of the second fruit.

That is to say, by illuminating and comprehending the false imaginings regarding the phenomenal marks of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), one differs from those at the first fruit who practice the fourfold contemplation; therefore, it receives the name "sudden" (*tun*).

The characteristic of arising is the various fetters; the characteristic of seeing is false discrimination. When these two do not arise, and one cultivates meditative concentration solely through untainted wisdom, then one will clearly perceive the characteristics of the path to dhyāna.
Advancing to sever the afflictions of desire within the realm of desire until six grades are exhausted, with only one more birth remaining, it is said that they "suddenly come to this world.
To reach the end of suffering means to transcend the cycle of birth and death among human beings.
"One who attains nirvana" refers to one who realizes the second fruit.
"Mahāmati, what is an anāgāmin?"

It refers to one who, having seen the faults of the arising of the characteristics and the nature—or the lack of nature—of form in the past, future, and present, causes false conceptualization not to arise and severs the fetters; therefore, they are called an Anāgāmin.
These three types of fruit-realizers universally observe that the forms and characteristics of the three periods of time are all empty; it is not that their intrinsic nature is itself empty.
Because they have departed from the faults and afflictions of dualistic discrimination regarding existence and non-existence, it is said that "delusive thoughts do not arise."
"Severing the fetters" refers to severing the final three grades of deluded afflictions (*kleśa*) within the desire realm. "Mahāmati!

An Arhat is so called because of the various dhyānas, samādhis, powers of liberation, and insights; it is because afflictions, suffering, and false conceptualizations have no inherent nature that one is named an Arhat."
"The various dhyānas and samādhis refer to the wisdom and concentration cultivated by the arhats.
Liberation, power, and clarity refer to the dharmas realized therein.
Power refers to the supernormal powers (abhijñā), while clarity refers to the three types of higher knowledge (vidyā)."

By means of this, one clearly realizes that the afflictions, various sufferings, and all discriminations are empty; that is to say, when the delusions of thought within the realms of form and formlessness are completely purified, one realizes the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!"
The World-Honored One has spoken of three kinds of arhats; which of these does this discourse refer to?
World-Honored One, are you speaking of the path of the single vehicle of tranquility?
"Is this a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva manifesting through skillful means as an Arhat,
or is it a transformation created by a Buddha?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“Only the śrāvakas who have attained the path of the single vehicle of tranquility [are so];

it is not others. Others—those practicing the bodhisattva path and those who are emanations of the Buddha—manifest birth within the great assembly due to their skillful means and original vows, in order to adorn the Buddha’s retinue.”
Mahāmati! Within the realm of conceptual construction, various teachings are expounded, such as the attainment of fruits and the attainment of dhyāna.

Because one has utterly transcended entering dhyāna, the manifestation of the realization that all is but the appearance of one's own mind is designated by the term "attainment of fruit. Thus it is called the attainment of fruit.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!
Those who wish to transcend the realms of dhyāna, the immeasurables, and the formless should abandon the marks of what is manifested by their own minds. Mahāmati!
It is not the case that one who has attained the meditative absorption of sensation and perception transcends the direct manifestation of their own mind.
Why? Because there is the measure of mind (cittamātra).
Regarding these Arhats, their names and characteristics may be considered both general and specific. Generally, they are all termed "Arhats"; specifically, there are three distinct types.
Among these three, one is real and two are provisional. Those who have attained the path of the single vehicle of tranquility are the real;
those who are bodhisattvas manifesting through skillful means, as well as those emanated by Buddhas, are the two provisional types.
The Buddha replied that the Arhats mentioned are real and not provisional.
As for the "One Vehicle," it refers to one of the three vehicles, not the One Vehicle of the Buddha-vehicle itself.

Regarding the "skillful means and original vows," these refer to the other two types [of Arhats]: those who, having previously made vows of skillful means, manifest as Arhats to adorn the Buddha’s assembly and serve as his retinue.

He preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings who are caught in false conceptualization and practices together with them in their cultivation and realization; therefore, it is said that he attains the fruits and attains dhyāna.
Although he enters into dhyāna, he does not abide in dhyāna; likewise, according to the measure of the mind, he manifests the attainment of the fruits but does not abide in those fruits.

Since these two kinds of provisional practice differ from actual practice and do not abide in the fruits or in meditative absorption, they constitute "transcending dhyāna. Thus, by demonstrating the characteristics of transcending dhyāna, he causes them to abandon mundane dhyāna and attain supramundane dhyāna.
Worldly dhyāna refers to the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions.
That which transcends one's own mind occurs when the scope of the mind reaches its ultimate limit; this is precisely Tathāgata-dhyāna.
If that is so, then is not the cessation of perception and feeling (nirodhasamāpatti) the transcendence of the mind-measure (cittamātra)?
Therefore, [the text] again clarifies: "It is not so.
Because the grasping for the cessation of perception and feeling is itself also the mind-measure, one must relinquish everything, for nothing can be apprehended.
This is precisely what is meant in the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* when it says: "The illumination and that which illuminates are simultaneously extinguished in stillness.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The various dhyānas and the four immeasurables, The formless attainments and samādhis,"
When all sensation and perception cease, even the "mind-only" does not exist there.
The fruits of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, and anāgāmin,
as well as arhatship— all these are delusions of the mind.
"Meditator, meditation, and its objects— By severing these, one perceives the ultimate truth.
These are merely the measure of deluded thought; If one awakens to this, there is liberation.
In this verse, the first four lines praise the aforementioned transcendence of the stages of dhyāna, while the middle four lines praise the aforementioned four fruits of the śrāvaka path.

Regarding "delusion": this uses the Great Vehicle to refute the Small Vehicle, meaning that even the grasping at the marks of *nirvāṇa* by those of the Small Vehicle is a delusive mental construction.

The latter four lines concern "dhyāna" and so forth; that is, the aforementioned "enterer" and "that which is entered," as well as the objects of focus for dhyāna, the abandonment of the origin [of suffering], the knowledge of suffering, and the vision of the principle of the True Dharma—all these are merely the conceptualized mind-measure within the nature of quiescent extinction.
If one can awaken to this, then there is ultimate liberation; it is an attainment through non-attainment.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are two kinds of awakening:
namely, the awakening of discernment, and the awakening that establishes through the grasping and attachment to the marks of false imagination."
Mahāmati!

As for "discerning awareness," it refers to the discernment that the self-nature and characteristics of phenomena cannot be apprehended when analyzed through the four logical alternatives; this is called discerning awareness.
The text above states that because awakening leads to liberation, it further teaches the path of awakening.

Regarding the two meanings of awakening, although they may at first glance appear to differ as "true" and "false," according to the concluding passage which says, "the Bodhisattva achieves [them]," both are objects of contemplation for the Great Being (Mahāsattva), differing only in their conventional and ultimate aspects.
The awakening of contemplative observation is the awakening of ultimate truth, while the awakening of establishment is the awakening of conventional truth.
This is because the Bodhisattva contemplates the ultimate without abandoning the conventional, and illuminates the conventional without contradicting the ultimate.

Regarding the phrase "if the nature of awakening is itself the self-nature," this refers to contemplating the self-nature of all phenomena. This nature is primordially devoid of characteristics and cannot be analyzed or discriminated through the four logical alternatives, such as identity or difference; therefore, it is said to be "unobtainable."

“Mahāmati! As for those four positions, they refer to being free from identity and difference, bothness and not-bothness, existence and non-existence, and neither-existence-nor-non-existence, as well as permanence and impermanence; these are called the four positions.”
Mahāmati!
This freedom from these four positions is called "all dharmas.
Mahāmati!
"One should study and practice this fourfold observation of all phenomena.
The characteristics of these four propositions are as explained previously.
As for "being free from the four propositions," it means not being attached to false conceptualizations.
If one falls into the calculations of the four propositions, this is not the realization of the self-nature of the awakened nature.
Now, since all these are sought and found to be unobtainable, one departs from those four propositions and returns to the original nature; this is called "all dharmas."

By observing all phenomena through these four lines, there is no insentient thing that is not included and no nature that is not revealed; therefore, the exhortation concludes: "One should practice and study."
“Mahāmati, what is the awakening that establishes through the grasping and attachment to the characteristics of false discrimination?

It refers to the grasping of the characteristics of false discrimination, and the attachment to the unreal characteristics of the four great elements—solidity, moisture, heat, and motion—as well as the attachment to propositions, reasons, and examples; thus one establishes what is established upon the unreal. This is called the awakening that establishes through the grasping and attachment to the characteristics of false discrimination.”
These are called the two aspects of awakening.

If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva accomplishes these two aspects of awakening—the aspect of the selflessness of persons and phenomena—and thoroughly understands through skillful means the awakening to non-existence, they will observe the stages of practice, attain the first stage (*bhūmi*), enter into one hundred samādhis, and obtain the distinguished samādhis. They will see one hundred Buddhas and one hundred Bodhisattvas, know the events of one hundred kalpas in both the past and the future, illuminate one hundred lands, and understand the characteristics of the successive higher stages. With their great vows being preeminent and their spiritual powers being sovereign, they will receive the consecration of the Cloud of Dharma and shall attain the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-awakening.

Skillfully binding the mind to the ten inexhaustible phrases, they bring sentient beings to maturity; adorned with various transformations and radiant light, they attain the samādhi of the noble bliss of self-awakening.
Second, regarding the establishment of awakening, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:

"To grasp at the characteristics of the various great elements—solidity, moisture, heat, and motion—and to become attached to them through false conceptualization, establishing them falsely by means of propositions, reasons, and examples; this is called the wisdom of attachment to the establishment of conceptualizing characteristics."

The thesis (*pakṣa*), reason (*hetu*), and example (*dṛṣṭānta*) constitute the five-membered syllogism; although these are established as unreal constructs, they are nonetheless posited by virtue of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Thus, the two modes of reality—the ultimate and the conventional—do not obstruct one another.
The phrase "If a bodhisattva... below summarizes the characteristics of the accomplishment of the two types of awakening.
Because the first awakening is accomplished, one knows the characteristic of selflessness regarding persons and phenomena;

because the subsequent awakening is accomplished, one realizes that the characteristic of selflessness is not separate from persons and phenomena; therefore, it is said that one ultimately and skillfully knows the means (*upāya*).

Regarding the realization of "nothingness," one must first pass through the stages of practice by means of two kinds of contemplative observation (*vitarka-vicāra*) before attaining entry into the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*).

As for the statement that entering samādhi, seeing the Buddha, and so forth are all described in terms of "a hundred," it is because when a bodhisattva first shatters ignorance, they are able to manifest bodies throughout a hundred worlds, and the number of dharma-gates they enter is likewise equal to that. Thus, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"When a bodhisattva enters the First Ground, they realize ten hundred gates of clarity."
First, in a single instant, one realizes a hundred samādhis;
second, with the purified divine eye, one sees a hundred buddha-fields;
third, by means of supernormal powers, one can shake a hundred buddha-worlds.
Fourth, one is able to travel to a hundred Buddha-worlds to teach and transform sentient beings;
fifth, one is able to manifest a hundred types of physical forms from a single body so that sentient beings may see them;
sixth, one is able to bring to maturity a hundred types of sentient beings who are to be transformed.
Seventh, for the sake of benefiting others, he is able to remain in the world by sustaining his physical body for a hundred kalpas;
eighth, he is able to know the events of a hundred kalpas across the past and future limits;
ninth, he is able to enter the gate of illumination of the hundred dharmas through wisdom, penetrating and understanding them thoroughly.
Tenth, one is able to observe a hundred classes of kinsmen through the body.
On the subsequent stages, these qualities increase and become increasingly superior.

Regarding the ten inexhaustible phrases, as stated in the "Ten Stages" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, when dwelling in the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), there are ten inexhaustible phrases, and so forth.
It is also like the ten practices and vows of Samantabhadra, all of which speak of inexhaustibility.
By binding the mind with these virtues, one brings sentient beings to maturity until they reach the samādhi of the noble bliss of self-awakening; thus, the bodhisattva’s task is complete.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati,
a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should be skilled in the four great elements and derived form.
How is a bodhisattva skilled in the four great elements and derived form?"
Mahāmati!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva awakens in this way, they realize that those ultimate truths consist of the non-arising of the four great elements; they thus observe the non-arising of those four great elements.

Having observed this, one realizes the limits of name-and-form (nāma-rūpa) and conceptual construction (vikalpa), as well as the limits of what is manifested by one's own mind; that external objects have no intrinsic nature—this is called the limit of conceptual construction manifested by the mind.

This refers to the three realms; one contemplates the nature of the derived matter produced by the four great elements as being free from the four propositions and universally pure. Being devoid of self and what belongs to self, it abides in its own specific characteristics and segments according to the true reality, with its unarisen specific characteristics thus established.
The preceding [passage] stated that the four great elements have not yet been fully explained; therefore, they are presented again here.
First, to clarify the capacity for contemplation and observation, it says: "The Bodhisattva performs such contemplation," and so forth.

To say that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) do not arise in ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is a matter of principle; furthermore, this is spoken in continuation of the preceding observation of awakening (*bodhi*).

However, it is not that principle lacks the four great elements; rather, it directly reveals their signlessness (*animitta*), and thus they are said to be "unborn. This is why the Bodhisattva performs the observation of non-arising.

Arising from non-arising, this is the source of the arising of the four great elements; therefore, there exist the names, characteristics, and conceptualizations of these four great elements in succession.

When one investigates the origin of these four great elements, they too are merely the manifestations of one's own mind. Once it is realized that all phenomena are mind-only, one attains the understanding that external natures lack inherent existence; thus, one contemplates that the nature of the derived matter of those four great elements is fundamentally detached.

"Nature is detached" refers to the fourfold negation of arising (*catuskoṭi*). By means of these four negations, one thoroughly purifies the four great elements; this is also the four great elements being perfectly detached from the four natures.

Through this detachment from "self" and "what belongs to self," one returns to the original state. Because one returns to the original state, each phenomenon (*dharma*) does not lose its own essence; therefore it is said: "The true mark abides in its own characteristics and distinct divisions."

In accordance with the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), characteristics are identical as one; yet when self-characteristics are divided into segments, there are distinctions. Because this identity and difference do not obstruct one another, the unarisen self-characteristics are thus established—this is the wisdom that is capable of awakening.
“Mahāmati! How do those four great elements give rise to derived matter (*bhautika*)?

It is said that the great element of the delusion of moisture gives rise to the internal and external water element; the great element of the delusion of capability gives rise to the internal and external fire element; the great element of the delusion of movement gives rise to the internal and external wind element; and the great element of the delusion of cutting and fragmenting form gives rise to the internal and external earth element.”
"When form and space coexist, one becomes attached to false truths; the five aggregates gather, and the derived matter of the four great elements arises.
This clarifies the phenomena that are perceived.
Furthermore, building upon the preceding text, he investigates and explains its characteristics:

regarding those "four great elements" (mahābhūta), from the perspective of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), the four great elements are taken as "that"; yet from the perspective of the four great elements themselves, the ultimate truth is likewise taken as "that."

Regarding the statement that the four great elements give rise to derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*): the great elements act as the "producers," as previously described in terms of solidity, moisture, heat, and motion;
the four elements act as the "produced," as subsequently described in terms of the internal and external water elements and so forth, which are collectively termed "matter."

In the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, however, they arise interactively, as it says: "Awakened clarity and the dullness of space depend upon one another to form agitation; thus there is the wind-circle," and so forth.

Now, as each is produced according to its own category, there arise moist great elements (*mahābhūta*) from the water element and so forth; thus, while the phrasing may differ, the underlying principle is consistent. Regarding the method of their production:

none fail to possess characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) based on their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). From the subtle to the manifest, these characteristics are formed through conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) and do not arise independently of seeds (*bīja*); therefore, the generation of the myriad categories originates fundamentally from the single mind.
What are called moisture, adaptability, motion, and cohesion are each explained according to the specific characteristics of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

Furthermore, moisture and the others may also be discussed in terms of the divisions of greed, hatred, and delusion; thus, each is said to be "false conceptualization" (*vikalpa*) and "great variety" (*mahā-vicitra*). All of these arise from the subtle.

Once they have manifested, they constitute the four great elements of the internal and external; that is, the primary retribution is termed "internal" and the environmental retribution is termed "external. Both pervade all things and coexist with space; therefore, it says, "form and empty space," and so forth.
The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) cling to false truths herein, either calculating existence and non-existence or giving rise to fixed limits; these have already been refuted as before.

Because the derived matter (bhautika-rūpa) is produced from the four great elements (mahābhūta), there are the five aggregates (pañca-skandha); because of the aggregates, the six sense faculties (ṣaḍ-indriya) exist, arising in succession. Therefore, it is said that "derived matter is produced from the four great elements."
“Mahāmati! As for consciousness (vijñāna), because it takes pleasure in various objective realms (viṣaya), it continues into other realms of existence (gati).
Mahāmati!”

The four great elements such as earth and so forth, as well as the derived matter they produce, possess conditions that are the four great elements, yet they are not conditions for those [very] four great elements.
Why is this? It is because when there is no nature, no form-and-characteristic, no location, and no application of effort, the great elements do not arise.

Mahāmati! [The four great elements] arise from the conjunction of nature, form-and-characteristics, location, and the application of activity; they are not formless. Therefore, these characteristics of matter produced by the four great elements are the false imaginings of the non-Buddhists, not mine.
"Consciousness" refers to the six consciousnesses; because these six consciousnesses delight in various sensory objects, entering, exiting, and traversing them, they are called "traces.
This arises from deluded consciousness becoming attached to deluded objects, thereby forming karmic bonds and leading to rebirth within the six realms of existence in an uninterrupted succession.
Furthermore, the phrase "the earth and the other four great elements" indicates that the four great elements cannot create [form] alone; they must necessarily rely on conditions.
Since it does not depend exclusively on conditions, it is said: "it is not those four great elements as conditions."
The following section provides a detailed explanation of its meaning:
that is to say, the nature of moisture and so forth, as well as the physical characteristics, are the causes of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and their material forms;
the locations and the skillful means of their activity are the conditions (*pratyaya*).
If, by virtue of having the nature of non-arising, [the great elements] do not arise even when conditions are present, they are therefore said to be "unborn great elements.
Since form must necessarily be produced through the conjunction of various conditions and cannot exist without them, it likewise resides within those conditions.
Since there is neither being nor non-being, there is fundamentally no real nature; that which arises without a nature thus clarifies the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

As for the statement regarding the "delusive thoughts of externalists," this and the previous remark concerning attachment to false truths are both refutations; it means that the characteristics of the four great elements and derived matter are not the same as the delusive conceptualizations of externalists, and therefore it says, "not-self."
"Furthermore, Mahāmati,
I shall explain the characteristic of the intrinsic nature of the aggregates (*skandha*).
What is the characteristic of the intrinsic nature of the aggregates?
They are the five aggregates.
What are the five?
They are form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Those four aggregates are non-material; they are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Mahāmati, as for matter, it consists of the four great elements and their derived forms, each having distinct characteristics.
Mahāmati! It is not that formless things lack the number four, as is the case with space.
For example, although space transcends numerical characteristics and is free from numbers, through false conceptualization one speaks of "one space."
Mahāmati!
Thus, the characteristics of the aggregates transcend enumeration and are free from number; they are free from existence and non-existence, and free from the four propositions.
These characteristics of enumeration are the conventional speech of the foolish, not that of the noble ones.
This clarifies the characteristics of the intrinsic nature and the enumeration or non-enumeration of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Regarding "enumeration," since both the material (*rūpa*) and the immaterial (*arūpa*) each have four counts, it is said: "Those four aggregates are non-material."

Furthermore, it is said that as for "form" (rūpa), the derivative forms produced by the four great elements each have distinct characteristics; thus, while the four great elements themselves are not identical, they are collectively termed "form," and form itself also consists of four types.

Next, regarding the mention of "having numbers," both the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are not characterized by numbers. To illustrate this by way of the formless realm, it is said that there are no four numbers in the formless like those in space; this correctly states that the four aggregates (*skandha*) of the formless are fundamentally without the existence of four.
For example, just as space transcends all numerical characteristics, yet through false conceptualization and discrimination one says that space is "one," so too are the aggregates (skandhas).
They transcend all numerical characteristics and the four logical extremes of existence, non-existence, and so forth.

To calculate that there are a certain number of marks is the talk of ordinary worldlings, not that of the noble sages; as it is said: "The Buddha-body is unconditioned and does not fall into numerical categories."
“Mahāmati! The various forms and images of the noble ones are like illusions, free from the conceptualization of being either different or not different.
They are also like dreams, reflections, or the body of a person, because they are free from being either different or not different.”
Mahāmati! The noble wisdom that enters into the aggregates appears as the conceptualization of the same [aggregates]; this is called the characteristic of the self-nature of the aggregates.
You should eliminate it; having eliminated it, you shall preach the Dharma of tranquility and sever all the views of the non-Buddhists in all Buddha-fields.
Mahāmati! When tranquility is taught, the vision of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) is purified, and one enters the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*).

Having entered the Immovable Stage, one attains mastery over immeasurable samādhis and the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*), realizes the Illusion-like Samādhi (*māyopama-samādhi*) to its ultimate extent, and gains mastery over the powers (*bala*) and insights (*vidyā*). Thus, one rescues, gathers, and benefits all sentient beings; just as the great earth supports and nurtures all living beings, so too does the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva universally deliver all beings.

The Noble One realizes that the aggregates (skandhas) are like illusions; although they manifest in various forms and appearances, he is free from the views of designating them as either different or not different. Just as the body of a person appears within a dream or a reflection, yet lacks any substantial reality, how could there be anything that is either different or not different?

However, the views of difference and non-difference are merely the deluded imaginings of ordinary beings. The reason the Buddha is able to remain detached from them is that he realizes the essence of the aggregates (*skandha*) for both ordinary beings and sages is fundamentally non-dual; thus it is said: "The realm of noble wisdom is identical to the manifestation of the deluded imaginings of the aggregates."

If ordinary beings wish to restore their original nature, they must distance themselves from the false characteristics and natures of the aggregates; therefore, it is said, "You should eliminate them.
When deluded attachments are extinguished, quiescence is revealed, and thus one can once again expound this Dharma of quiescence, remaining far removed from all views of the heterodox paths.

When this Dharma is taught, having already become free from the grasping at a self-nature in phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), one is able to enter the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*) and attain immeasurable samādhis and all Dharma-gates, universally rescuing all classes of beings, just as the earth supports and nurtures all things.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati,
there are four kinds of nirvāṇa among the various non-Buddhists.
What are these four?

That is to say: the nirvana of the non-existence of the intrinsic nature of essence; the nirvana of the non-existence of various characteristics and essences; the nirvana of awakening to the non-existence of self-characteristics and intrinsic natures; and the nirvana of severing the continuous flow of the individual and common characteristics of the aggregates. These are called the four kinds of nirvana of the various non-Buddhists, and they are not the Dharma taught by me.
"Mahāmati!
What I have taught is that the cessation of the conceptualizing consciousness (*vikalpa-vijñāna*) is called nirvāṇa.
Regarding the teaching of nirvāṇa, there are both the heterodox and the orthodox; wishing to expound the orthodox, the Buddha first refutes the heterodox.

Regarding the four kinds of nirvana taught by non-Buddhists, their names and characteristics are as listed in the sutras. Nirvana is the fruit, and a fruit is obtained through its cause; since their cause is erroneous, their fruit is likewise not correct. Therefore, it is said: "This is not what I have taught."
What I call nirvana is simply the extinction of deluded consciousness.

This is because certain non-Buddhists maintain a nirvana that does not transcend the *ātman* (spiritual self); since this *ātman* is itself deluded consciousness, I counteract their view by teaching the extinction of such deluded, conceptualizing consciousness.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One,
do you not establish the eight consciousnesses?"
The Buddha said:
"It is established.
Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If it is established [that they are distinct], why is it that the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is excluded, and not the seven [sensory] consciousnesses?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“Because of their causes and because of their objects of perception, the seven consciousnesses do not arise.”

The manas-consciousness arises from the attachment to the segmentation of objects; it is nourished by habitual tendencies and coexists with the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) and the manas. It arises through the causal conditions of conceptualizing "self" and "what belongs to self," and does not destroy the characteristics of the body. Due to the storehouse consciousness, it clings to the objects manifested by one's own mind as its focal point, and as a collection of mental states, it arises through mutual causality.
It is like the waves of the ocean: when stirred by the wind of objects manifested from one's own mind, they arise and cease in the same way.
Therefore, when the *manovijñāna* ceases, the seven consciousnesses also cease.

The interlocutor said, "If the extinction of deluded conceptualization and consciousness is called nirvana, then one might suspect that the eight consciousnesses also perish. The Buddha answered that they do not perish.
He stated that what is established [as nirvana] is precisely their non-extinction.

Furthermore, there is doubt as to why the seventh consciousness does not cease. The Buddha answers that because it has those [six] as its cause and object of apprehension (*ālambana*), the seventh consciousness does not arise. These "causes and objects of apprehension" refer to the six consciousnesses; while the seventh consciousness clings to a self, it is never separated from them.
If the six consciousnesses cease, then the seventh consciousness likewise does not arise.

The section below on "consciousness" (vijñāna) generally demonstrates that the various consciousnesses arise through mutual dependence and never fail to coexist; they are thus one in essence yet distinct in their manifestations.
Furthermore, there are four intended meanings:
first, regarding the "segmentation of objects," this refers to the six consciousnesses arising from the six sense-objects.
2. Regarding "nurtured by habitual tendencies," this means that the six consciousnesses are not separate from the seventh and eighth consciousnesses;
3. Regarding "clinging to 'I' and 'mine'," this means that the ego-grasping of the seventh consciousness arises from contemplating its causes and conditions.

4. Regarding "the unchanging bodily characteristics" and below: the *ālayavijñāna* is the eighth consciousness. The statement "due to the攀緣 (*ālambana*) of objects manifested by one's own mind" means that these eight consciousnesses take the six consciousnesses as their cognitive conditions (*ālambaka*), and in turn take the objects manifested by their own minds—namely, the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). Because of clinging (*abhiniveśa*), the six consciousnesses arise; since they can aggregate all mental states, it is called "the arising of the collection of minds. This means that the eight consciousnesses and the six consciousnesses arise through mutual causality. Thus, in this mutual causality there is the root and the branches: the "root" refers to the eight consciousnesses transforming to produce the various [other] consciousnesses, while the "branches" refer to the six consciousnesses giving rise to both good and evil. The seventh consciousness transmits between them; therefore, it is said they are "mutually causal."

To further clarify this through analogy: the ocean represents the eight consciousnesses, and the waves represent the six consciousnesses. The winds of the objective spheres serve as the conditions; these spheres are, in fact, manifestations of one’s own mind. These winds blow upon the ocean of the eight consciousnesses, causing various consciousnesses to arise. Whether arising or ceasing, it is just like how wind depends upon the ocean and waves are stirred by the wind—their mutual, reciprocal relationship is exactly like this.
When the wind ceases, the waves subside; thus it is said, "When the mental consciousness ceases, the seven consciousnesses also cease.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
