"I am not of the nature of Nirvana, Neither in my activities nor in my marks."
The false imagination, the object-field, and consciousness—when these are extinguished, I am in nirvāṇa.
With that as cause and that as the object-condition, the mental faculty and so forth constitute the body;
that which provides the cause is the mind, serving as the support for consciousness.
"Just as when the great flow of water is exhausted, waves no longer arise;
so too, when the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) ceases, the various forms of consciousness do not arise.
The four kinds of nirvāṇa spoken of by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) do not transcend [the duality of] essence (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

Once the Buddha had rejected this, [the interlocutor] said: "I do not take nature (dharmatā) or characteristics (lakṣaṇa) as nirvāṇa; rather, I take the cessation of deluded thought, the cognitive obstructions, and consciousness as nirvāṇa.

Regarding such statements as "due to that cause and that object-condition," he explains that the seven consciousnesses arise from the mental tendencies and causes to form the six groups of consciousness. Yet, when one investigates their fundamental cause, it is ultimately the mind of the eighth consciousness that serves as the support for all the various consciousnesses.
As with the water below, the intended meaning can be seen through this analogy.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati,
I shall now explain the general characteristics of the discrimination of the self-nature of conceptual construction."

If you and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas thoroughly discern the common characteristics of the discrimination of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), you will transcend false imagination and attain the noble self-realization of the sages. You will clearly perceive the common path of the non-Buddhists, realize the grasped and the grasper within false imagination, sever the various marks of dependent origination and the activities of the imagined nature, and no longer engage in false imagination.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:

"I shall now explain the characteristics of the differentiation of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), so that you and all the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas may thoroughly understand this meaning, transcend all false imaginings, realize the realm of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), and know the teachings of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). By remaining far removed from the discrimination of grasper and grasped (*grāhya-grāhaka-vikalpa*), you shall no longer further cling to the imagined characteristics within the various manifestations of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)."
“Mahāmati! What is the common characteristic of the discrimination of the self-nature of false imagination?

It refers to: the false imagination of verbal expression, the false imagination of the object expressed, the false imagination of marks, the false imagination of benefit, the false imagination of self-nature, the false imagination of cause, the false imagination of views, the false imagination of accomplishment, the false imagination of birth, the false imagination of non-birth, the false imagination of continuity, and the false imagination of bondage and non-bondage. These are called the common characteristics of the discrimination of the self-nature of false imagination.”
"Delusive conceptualization is one, yet it varies according to its objects; herein, first the general and then the specific are presented. The general name is 'the visible.
There are twelve specific aspects: first, the twelve names are listed, followed by an inquiry into and explanation of their meanings."
“Mahāmati! What is the discrimination of verbal expression?
It refers to the attachment to various exquisite sounds, songs, and melodies; this is called the discrimination of verbal expression.”
"This is the attachment to various sounds, words, and phrases, taking them to possess an intrinsic nature. Mahāmati,
what is the discrimination of the objects spoken of?"

It refers to the intrinsic nature of the object that is spoken of, which is known by noble wisdom; based upon that, verbal conceptualization arises. This is called the conceptualization of the object that is spoken of.

Regarding the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the things spoken of: whatever things are spoken of, their ultimate intrinsic nature is known only by noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*); ordinary fools do not understand this, but merely give rise to verbal conceptualization (*prapañca-vikalpa*) based upon those things.
“Mahāmati, what is the discrimination of characteristics?

It refers to the attachment to those very things already mentioned, such as the various attachments based on the delusion of a mirage—namely, the discrimination of all natures regarding the characteristics of solidity, moisture, heat, and motion. This is called the discrimination of characteristics.”

These words arise from views based on specific phenomena, like a thirsty deer rushing toward a mirage while perceiving it as water; that is, to cling to earth, water, fire, and wind as having the natures of solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion, without knowing that their nature is fundamentally integrated, and thus to falsely calculate names and marks regarding all dharmas.
Nature is itself the Dharma.
"Mahāmati! What is the discrimination of benefit?
"To take pleasure in various kinds of gold, silver, and precious jewels is called 'deluded discrimination regarding gain.
Worldly wealth and treasures are fundamentally illusory things, yet ordinary people, failing to understand this, give rise to craving and attachment."
“Mahāmati! What is the discrimination of intrinsic nature?
It refers to maintaining that ‘this is exactly thus’ and not otherwise; such erroneous views and discriminations are called the discrimination of intrinsic nature.”

Regarding the phrase "holding this thus," "holding" means grasping; it refers to giving rise to the view of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) toward all phenomena, grasping them as being thus and regarding everything else as being otherwise. How does this differ from the false views and conceptualizations of the non-Buddhists?
“Mahāmati! What is causal conceptualization?
It refers to the arising of the marks of causal characteristics through the discrimination of cause and condition as being either existent or non-existent; this is called causal conceptualization.”

This means that giving rise to views such as existence and non-existence regarding phenomena produced by causes and conditions, and engaging in conceptual discrimination, constitutes the cause of birth and death.
"Mahāmati, what is the discrimination of views?"

"It refers to the evil views of existence and non-existence, identity and difference, both and neither; these are the deluded imaginings and attachments of externalists. This is called the 'delusion of views.
This states that the evil views of externalists consist of clinging to the fourfold conceptual distinctions of existence, non-existence, identity, difference, both, and neither.
“Mahāmati! What is the conceptualization of establishment?
It refers to the formation of a definitive doctrine based on the notions of ‘self’ and ‘what belongs to self’; this is called the conceptualization of establishment.”
"This refers to the conceptualization and verbal expression that conceives of a self and what belongs to a self upon the basis of provisional designations and real dharmas.
Mahāmati, what is the discrimination of arising?"
"It refers to the conceptual attachment arising from taking the nature of existence and non-existence as an object;
this is called the discrimination of origination. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"To reckon that all phenomena, whether existent or non-existent, arise from conditions—this is called the discrimination of origination."
“Mahāmati! What is the delusion of non-arising?
It refers to the fact that all natures are fundamentally unarisen; because there is no causal seed, an uncaused body arises. This is called the delusion of non-arising.”

This means that if all phenomena possessed an intrinsic nature prior to the existence of their various conditions, they would not depend on causes and conditions for their arising; therefore, one gives rise to the discrimination of non-arising.
“Mahāmati! What is the discrimination of continuity?
It refers to their mutual continuity, like gold and its thread; this is called the discrimination of continuity.”
Regarding the phrase "their mutual continuity is like gold and thread," the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"That this and that are mutually interconnected, like gold and thread—this is called the discrimination of continuity."
“Mahāmati, what is the discrimination of bondage and non-bondage?

It refers to the attachment to the causes and conditions of bondage and non-bondage, such as a person’s skillful means in either binding or releasing; this is called the discrimination of bondage and non-bondage.”
Regarding the attachment to the causal conditions of bondage and non-bondage: speaking in terms of principle, dharmas are fundamentally detached from the outset; what bondage could there be?
Yet, because emotional attachment constitutes bondage, one cannot say it does not exist.
Regarding the "person," the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:

"It is like a person who, through the skillful means of a rope, first binds [something] and then unties it; this is the conceptual attachment that arises within that which is neither bound nor liberated."
"In this general characteristic of the discrimination of the nature of false imagination, all foolish commoners cling to existence and non-existence.
This concludes the passage, as the various aforementioned attachments do not go beyond existence and non-existence.

“Mahāmati! Those who are attached to dependent origination and cling to it give rise to various kinds of false conceptualizations regarding intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Just as a magical illusion manifests various bodies, ordinary people, through their false conceptualizations, perceive various different illusions.”
Mahāmati! Illusion and its various manifestations are neither different nor non-different.
If they were different, illusion would not be the cause of those various manifestations.
If they were not different, there would be no distinction between illusion and its various manifestations, yet a distinction is perceived; therefore, they are neither different nor non-different.
For this reason, Mahāmati!

"You and the other Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should not cling to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) of illusory dependent origination as being either different or non-different, or as existing or non-existing.

Previously, the imagined nature was directly analyzed, yet it had not been clarified what it is that one clings to; therefore, dependent origination is now explained next, further illustrated by the metaphor of an illusion, to demonstrate that the imagined nature is fundamentally empty.

Ordinary beings do not understand this and perceive various distinct characteristics; therefore, it is said through analogy that "the illusion and the various [phenomena] are neither different nor non-different. This has been repeatedly examined and demonstrated, as can be seen from what was set forth previously.

If one realizes that phenomena lack intrinsic nature, then within dependent origination, conceptual constructions are entirely unapprehendable; therefore, one should not form attachments to them as being either different or non-different, or as existing or non-existing.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The mind is bound by its objects; perceptual conceptions and cognition follow along with them."
Non-existence and excellence arise from equalizing wisdom.
The self-nature of false conceptualization exists, yet it does not exist within dependent origination;
false conceptualization may be grasped, but dependent origination is not false conceptualization.
"The various constituent parts arise, yet like an illusion they are not established;
their characteristics are manifold, yet through false conceptualization they are not established.

As for "the mind being bound," it means that the present momentary thought is turned by sensory objects, thereby resulting in the bondage of karma; consequently, the originally inherent awakened wisdom also follows along with the delusion.
If one realizes that the false is itself the true and becomes detached from all marks of existence, then upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood, one possesses again the great wisdom of equality.
"Supreme" means most excellent; it refers to abiding in the stage of Buddhahood.
The eight lines following "the nature of false discrimination" discuss whether the dependent origination of false discrimination exists or does not exist.

The first four lines refer to the phenomena (*dharma*), while the latter four lines refer to analogies. This means that if the nature of false discrimination were to exist inherently, then no phenomena of dependent origination could be found, nor would false discrimination need to be established in dependence upon dependent origination.

If it were the case that false conceptualization could grasp and take up those objects such that they become false conceptualization, then since dependent origination itself is not false conceptualization, how could it ever become false conceptualization?

The analogy refers to a phantom person created by magic with various limbs: if these had already arisen prior to the magic, they would not depend upon the magic to be formed. Although those illusory appearances are manifold, the deluded imagination itself is not manifold; therefore, it is said that [the self] is not established. All of this demonstrates that neither existence nor non-existence can be apprehended.
“Those characteristics are indeed errors, all arising from the bonds of the mind;
through deluded conceptualization there is no true knowledge, for one conceptualizes within dependent origination.
The nature of these various conceptualizations is itself that very dependent origination.”
"Delusive thoughts are of many kinds; they arise from the delusion regarding dependent origination.
These eight lines further state that the characteristics of the delusion regarding dependent origination are formed through mutual causality.

Regarding the phrase "the faults of those characteristics," this refers to the faults of the characteristics of dependent origination; these faults are formed because the mind is bound by attachment, and this mental bondage is precisely delusive thought (*vikalpa*).

If one thoroughly understands dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), there will be no delusive conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Because of delusive conceptualization, one fails to awaken; thus, various discriminations arise within dependent origination. This dependent origination and delusive conceptualization exist in mutual dependence; from the very beginning, there is no distinction of priority or posteriority. Therefore, it is said that delusive conceptualization is itself dependent origination; their essence is certainly non-dual, yet ultimately, through dependent origination, discrimination exists.
“Conventional truth and ultimate truth—the third is birth without cause.
Conventional truth is spoken of through false conceptualization; its cessation is the realm of the sages.”
The conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is the worldly truth;
the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is the true truth.

The Buddhas always rely upon these two truths when teaching the Dharma; anything beyond these is the false conceptualization of non-Buddhists, which is why it is said that "a third [truth] arises without cause."
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"That which is known by those who have transcended the world is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); that which is known by worldly people is called conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The non-Buddhists establish twenty-five truths, clarifying that the effect exists within the cause.
First, from the primordial darkness arises awakening;
second, from awakening arises the mind of self;
third, from the mind of self arise form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and so forth. This is what is called "without cause," namely, the nature of spontaneity (*svabhāva*).
Following the refutation of false conceptualization, the three kinds of self-nature are established.
"Worldly truth" refers to the two kinds of self-nature: dependent origination and false conceptualization.
"The realm of the sages" refers to the perfected self-nature, which is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

However, when one is deluded regarding it, it is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); when one awakens to it, it is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Therefore, it is said: "When severed, it is the realm of the sages.
"Just as in the practice of cultivation, A single thing appears as manifold;
Yet within that, there is no manifoldness— Such is the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)."
Just as various cataracts cause the false imagination of manifold forms to appear,
yet the cataract itself is neither form nor non-form, so too it is through the failure to realize dependent origination that such appearances arise.
Just as refined pure gold is far removed from all impurities.
"As the void is free from clouds and mists, so too is the purity of delusive thought.
These four metaphors illustrate, first, the self-nature of delusive thought (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Regarding the matter of practice: it is like the ten *kṛtsnāyatana* (all-pervading bases) in dhyāna, wherein blue, yellow, red, white, and so forth, all pervade everywhere. Their objective realm is fundamentally one, yet through the power of mental conception, they appear in various forms; the characteristics of delusive thought are likewise thus.

Next, the passage following "various cataracts" serves as a metaphor for the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). Cataracts originally have no color, yet colors appear through deluded vision; thus, there is neither non-color nor color in reality. The same applies to the failure to realize dependent origination.
Furthermore, the two metaphors of refined gold and cloudless space both illustrate the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

To say that the two types of self-nature—those of deluded conceptualization (*parikalpita*) and dependent origination (*paratantra*)—are absent is like gold being free from dross and space being free from obscuration; therefore, it is said: "The purification of deluded conceptualization is likewise so."
"There is no nature of false imagination, yet there is that which arises through conditions.
Both establishment and denial are entirely destroyed by false imagination.
If false imagination lacked a nature, yet the nature of dependent origination existed,"
Absence of nature yet presence of nature; from the presence of nature, the absence of nature arises.
Depending upon false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), one attains that dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*);
sign (*nimitta*) and name (*nāman*) constantly follow one another, giving rise to all manner of false conceptualizations.
"Ultimately unestablished, one then transcends all delusive imaginings;
thereafter, wisdom is purified—this is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
This passage, beginning with "there being no nature of delusive imaginings," reiterates that the dependent origination of the imagined nature is fundamentally neither existent nor non-existent.

To assert that [things] definitely exist is to fall into the error of reification (*samāropa*); to assert that they definitely do not exist is to fall into the error of denial (*apavāda*). Both result from deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*) which destroys right view.

Regarding the statement that "if deluded conceptualization were non-existent, etc.": this means that if the nature of deluded conceptualization did not exist while the nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*) did exist, then existence would arise from non-existence, resulting in the fault of causelessness (*ahetuka-doṣa*).

Indeed, dependent origination arises from beginningless deluded thoughts and discriminations; yet these deluded thoughts depend upon names and appearances for their basis. Names and appearances follow one another like shadows following forms, and both are entirely false and illusory. It is because of failing to understand this that deluded thoughts arise.

When one exhausts the source of delusion and finds nothing established therein, then false conceptualization ceases of its own accord; this restoration of self-awakened noble wisdom is called the primary truth (*paramārtha*).
"Transcending" (*tīrṇa*) means precisely this cessation.
“There are twelve kinds of conceptual construction, and six kinds of dependent origination;
when one personally realizes the *jñeya* (the knowable), there is no distinction between them.
The five dharmas constitute reality, and self-nature is of three kinds.”
"Practicing the discernment of this does not transcend suchness.
The twelve types of false conceptualization are as previously explained.

Regarding the sixfold dependent origination, "six" refers to the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*); that is, the nature of dependent origination arises when it is stirred by the winds of the six objective spheres.
Some may claim that there are six causes; this is incorrect.
However, these deluded thoughts and dependent origination are all merely marks of differentiation; within the noble wisdom of self-awakening, there are no such differentiations.
This "clarity" (er-ming) is precisely wisdom.

The five dharmas and the three natures are all the Tathāgata’s methods for self-cultivation and transforming others; when a practitioner contemplates them in accordance with their true nature, there is nothing that is not the single principle of reality. Therefore, it is said: "It does not transcend suchness."
“The various marks and dependent origination—these are called the arising of false discrimination.
Those various marks of false discrimination arise from that dependent origination.
When awakened wisdom observes skillfully, there is neither dependent origination nor false discrimination.”
Once accomplished, there is no inherent nature; how then could there be the awakening of false imagination?
That imagined self-nature establishes the two other natures;
the various manifestations of false imagination are the pure realm of the noble ones.
Delusive thought is like painted colors; one calculates delusive thought based on dependent origination.
If it were different from delusive thought, it would rely upon the treatises of external paths.
Delusive thought speaks of that which is conceived; it arises from the conjunction of views.
"One who is free from these two kinds of false imagination—such a one shall attain realization.

Both characteristics and names are dependent origination; those names and characteristics are all false imaginings, and this dependent origination of false imagination arises entirely from names and characteristics.

Furthermore, when it is said that deluded thoughts arise from conditions, this refers to the fact that the deluded thoughts presently arising are produced from the conjunction of the sense organs and their objects.

Conversely, when it was stated above that dependent origination arises from deluded thoughts, this refers to how, through the delusion of the True, there come to be dharmas born of causes and conditions based on the unreal; students must examine these points with care.
However, when observed with correct wisdom, both are non-existent.

Regarding the statement that "once established, there is no inherent nature," this means that within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), there is fundamentally no grasping at a nature; how then could sentient beings give rise to deluded conceptualizations and cognitions?
Since one is deluded regarding true nature and gives rise to false conceptualization, there are two kinds of self-nature:

the self-nature of names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa-svabhāva*) and the self-nature of phenomena (*vastu-lakṣaṇa-svabhāva*). When one is deluded, various appearances manifest; when one awakens, this is the pure realm traversed by the sages.
"Deluded thoughts are like painted colors" means that existence arises within non-arising, just as originally there were no forms or images, yet they come into being because of painting.

Deluded thoughts are rooted in dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and dependent origination is rooted in discrimination (*vikalpa*). One calculates dependent origination and thereby gives rise to deluded thoughts; such is the nature of deluded thought.
That my Buddha taught through such skillful means was for the purpose of causing beings to turn back from delusion and return to the truth.

To speak of "delusive thought" in any way other than this would be the false calculations and frivolous arguments of non-Buddhist outsiders; therefore it is said: "Delusive thought speaks of what is conceived; it arises due to the conjunction of views."

"Indeed, the heterodox teachers employ their deluded minds to differentiate the characteristics of false conceptualization and to argue that [phenomena] arise from the conjunction of the three conditions; all of these are not correct doctrines.
If one is free from both dependent origination and false conceptualization, as well as the two kinds of self-nature, then that is the perfected nature."
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I only pray that you will explain for me the characteristics of the noble wisdom of self-realization and the Single Vehicle."

If one speaks of the characteristics of the noble wisdom of self-realization and the One Vehicle, I and other bodhisattvas have well realized the characteristics of the noble wisdom of self-realization and the One Vehicle; we have attained penetration into the Buddha-dharma not by depending on others.

Having heard the above, which exhaustively elucidates all delusions to reveal the ultimate truth (paramārtha), Mahāmati requested [the Buddha] for the sake of the assembly regarding the characteristics of self-realized noble wisdom and the characteristics of the One Vehicle, so as to contemplate, cultivate, and realize them.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!"
"Reflect upon this well; I shall speak for your sake.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "So be it;
I shall receive your instruction."
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"That which was known by the former sages and transmitted from one to another consists of the absence of intrinsic nature in false discrimination (*vikalpa*).

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells alone in a quiet place, observes through self-awakening, does not rely on others, and leaves behind the false discriminations of views, ascending higher and higher until entering the stage of the Tathāgata—this is called the characteristic of the noble wisdom of self-awakening."

What was known by the former sages consists of the characteristics of the practice of self-realized noble wisdom and the characteristics of the practice of the One Vehicle. This means that there have been no Buddhas of the past who did not attain perfect enlightenment through these two modes of practice; because they transmitted them to one another, this is precisely what is meant by "Buddha-to-Buddha transmission" and "patriarch-to-patriarch succession."
This constitutes a general response to the preceding inquiry.

From the passage "delusive thoughts lack intrinsic nature" (*parikalpita-niḥsvabhāva*) onwards, there is a specific response concerning the characteristics of the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*).

All phenomena are originally quiescent; however, the ignorant and foolish, failing to realize this, give rise to delusion. While they speak through conceptual discrimination, delusive phenomena fundamentally lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

However, if one wishes to advance in the cultivation of sublime practices, one must observe oneself in a quiet place; by observing without ceasing, all delusive thoughts will be separated from their attachments without effort. Gradually traversing the various stages (*bhūmi*), one enters the realm of the Tathāgata, which is what is called the spontaneous perfection of the noble wisdom of self-awakening.
“Mahāmati! What is the characteristic of the One Vehicle?
It is the awakening to the path of the One Vehicle; this is what I call the One Vehicle.”
What is the awakening to the path of the One Vehicle?
It is the non-arising of false conceptualization regarding the grasped and the grasper within the state of reality as it is; this is called the awakening of the One Vehicle, Mahāmati.

The realization of the One Vehicle cannot be attained by any others—such as non-Buddhists, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or even Brahmā kings—with the sole exception of the Tathāgata; for this reason, it is called the One Vehicle.
This explains the characteristics of the practice of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
What is called the "One Vehicle" is the Single Buddha Vehicle; it refers to the Mahāyāna Dharma that the Tathāgata rides upon.
This Dharma of the One Vehicle is not separate from the single mind of a person; that which is called the "wondrous Dharma" is precisely the mind itself.
For the mind is endowed with the wondrous Dharma, which is non-dual and indistinguishable from that realized by the Buddhas.
To wish to awaken to the path of the One Vehicle, one must investigate one’s own mind; hence it is said: "The false discrimination of the grasped and the grasper."

This means that by realizing the faculties and objects—the grasping subject and the grasped object—one’s deluded mind is immediately revealed as the true nature; abiding thus in accordance with reality, it is said: "In the state of suchness, one does not give rise to false conceptualization."
However, this path of awakening of the One Vehicle can be fully realized only by Buddha after Buddha; therefore, it is said that it cannot be attained by others, such as those of external paths.
Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Why do you teach the three vehicles and not the one vehicle?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Because they lack the nature for parinirvāṇa by their own power, I do not teach that all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas belong to a single vehicle."

Because all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas attain liberation through the skillful means of being tamed and granted tranquility by the Tathāgata, rather than by their own power, for this reason the One Vehicle is not taught [to them].
Furthermore, Mahāmati!
Because the afflictive obstructions and the habitual tendencies of karma have not been severed, I do not speak of a single vehicle for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Because they do not realize the selflessness of phenomena and have not transcended death by分段 (segmented) birth, I speak of three vehicles.

This question concerns the meaning behind the Tathāgata’s teaching of only the *Hīnayāna* and not the *Mahāyāna*. The Buddha answered that he did not teach the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) for three reasons.

First, regarding those whose nature is not to attain *parinirvāṇa* by themselves: because the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) are unable to realize that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is itself *nirvāṇa*, he did not teach it to them. This is the first reason.

Regarding the statement that they were "tamed" and granted "peace," it means that because they had received teachings on skillful means and cultivated the realization of emptiness and stillness, they were merely free from delusion and thus termed "liberated. However, as they had not yet attained all-encompassing liberation, [the Buddha] did not preach [the ultimate truth] to them; this is the second reason.

Regarding the mention of the "afflictive obstacles" (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and so forth: because [the Śrāvakas] have only severed the pervasive delusions of the four abodes (*catur-vāsabhūmi*) but have not yet severed the residual habits (*vāsanā*), and because their specific delusions remain entirely intact, [the Buddha] does not preach [the Mahāyāna] to them; this is the third reason.

The followers of the Two Vehicles have destroyed the attachment to a person (*pudgala-grāha*) but have not yet destroyed the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*); therefore, it is said that "they do not realize the selflessness of phenomena.

Although they have severed the afflictions (*kleśa*), they still abide within the stage of *paricchinna-bhava* (limited existence) and have not yet attained what is called *pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa* (transformative birth-and-death); therefore, it is said that "they are not free from limited death."
For the sake of those with such limited capacity, the Tathāgata has merely taught the Dharma of the Three Vehicles.
"Mahāmati! They have severed all afflictions, faults, and habitual tendencies, and they have realized the selflessness of phenomena."

Having severed all arising afflictions, faults, and habitual tendencies, and having realized that attachment to the savoring of the bliss of samādhi is not the true nature, they awaken to the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*). Having awakened, they further enter the supramundane, most excellent untainted realm, fulfill all requisites, and shall attain the Tathāgata’s inconceivable and sovereign Dharma-body.

This refers to the practitioner of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), who, having severed the habitual tendencies of afflictions (*kleśavāsanā*), is not intoxicated by ignorance; having realized the bliss of the samādhi of true emptiness, they do not give rise to attachment to its flavor, and thus it is said that they are "without nature" (*aniḥsvabhāva*) and attain awakening within the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*).

The untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*) refers to entering the Land of True Reward (*sambhoga-kāya*), receiving the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*), manifesting forms according to the capacities of beings, displaying birth and death, and delivering all from the realms of existence; therefore, it is said: "Having awakened, one further enters the supramundane."
Reaching the supreme Dharma-realm of Quiescent Light, fully endowed with the two adornments, one ultimately manifests the inconceivable and sovereign Dharmakāya; this is the One Buddha Vehicle.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“The vehicle of the devas and Brahmās, The vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas...”
The vehicles of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas—these various vehicles I have taught.
As long as the mind continues to function, these vehicles are not ultimate;
when that mind is extinguished, there is neither vehicle nor one who rides it.
"There is no establishment of vehicles; I teach them as the One Vehicle.
The first four lines generally praise all the vehicles, while the subsequent six lines praise the intent behind teaching the One Vehicle.

Regarding the statement "there is the turning of the mind," "turning" refers to activation; that is to say, if there is even a single thought-moment of movement, even the Buddha-vehicle is not ultimate, let alone the other vehicles.

It is said that where the movements of the mind cease, there is no one who can ride [the vehicle], nor is there any dharma that serves as the vehicle; even the Dharma-gate of the One Vehicle cannot be established. It is beyond names and transcends marks; it is neither negated nor affirmed. Only for those with such capacity is the One Vehicle taught.
“In order to guide sentient beings, I have distinguished and taught the various vehicles.
There are three kinds of liberation, as well as the selflessness of phenomena;
regarding afflictions and wisdom, in liberation they are both transcended.”
Just as a piece of wood floating on the ocean, Constantly turns with the rolling waves,
So too are the ignorant śrāvakas, Drifting and tossed by the winds of marks.
When their manifest afflictions arise and cease, They remain deluded by the afflictions of residual habits.
This verse explains the aforementioned teaching of the Three Vehicles.

The three kinds of liberation are the fruits realized by the Three Vehicles: namely, the Śrāvaka eliminates the active afflictions (kleśa), the Pratyekabuddha eliminates the residual impressions (vāsanā), and the Bodhisattva eliminates both the active afflictions and the residual impressions.
Although the destruction of delusions differs, the realization of the fruit is one: the *nirvāṇa* of true emptiness.

Regarding the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) and so forth, this refers to the Mahāyāna practitioner who attains the selflessness of phenomena; therein, afflictions and wisdom are equal, and bondage and liberation are non-dual—this constitutes the great liberation of being far removed from all attachments.

For example, this illustrates how those of the Two Vehicles have not yet severed the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and are thus tossed about by the winds of the mark of emptiness. They are like pieces of floating wood in the ocean, driven hither and thither by the waves; although they have severed the delusions that obstruct penetration, they have not yet severed fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*). Therefore, it is said they possess "the folly of residual habitual afflictions," wherein these "residual habits" are precisely ignorance.
“Delighting in the bliss of samādhi, Abiding in the untainted realm (anāsrava-dhātu),
There is no ultimate destination, Nor is there any returning back;
Having attained the body of various samādhis, They remain unawakened for as long as an eon.”
"Just as a person who is intoxicated awakens only after the wine has worn off, so too is the awakening to the Dharma: one attains the supreme body of a Buddha.

Those of the Two Vehicles, having departed from the suffering of分段生死 (paricchinna-janma-maraṇa, segmented birth and death) and attained the bliss of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and *nirvāṇa*, become attached to that state and fail to advance further; yet, they do not regress to the status of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
This body of samādhi falls into the pit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), remaining there without awakening even for the duration of an eon (*kalpa*).
It is like a person in the world who, having drunk wine, becomes intoxicated and confused, possessing no awareness at all; only when the alcohol has worn off does he subsequently awaken.
This metaphor illustrates the transformation of the faculties of the two vehicles and the mind’s turning toward the ultimate right gnosis that realizes the selflessness of phenomena;
therefore, it is said, "one attains the unsurpassed body of a Buddha. *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra-ṭīkā*, Fascicle Two, Part Two.
